rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Average power is V_rms I_rms times the power factor cosφ, and cosφ = R/Z. It is 1 at resonance and 0 in a pure reactor. A lagging power factor is inductive and is often corrected with capacitors.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Leading means capacitive. Lagging means inductive.  ·  Use rms values in the power formula.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: The average power in a series LCR circuit is V_rms I_rms cosφ, not the product of the rms voltage and current alone. The extra factor cosφ is the power factor.  ·  From the impedance triangle, cosφ = R/Z. A circuit that is almost a pure resistor has Z near R and a power factor near 1. A circuit dominated by reactance has a small power factor.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Power factor is cosφ.  ·  It equals R/Z.  ·  It is 1 at resonance.  ·  It is 0 for a pure L or C.

rows.label: Universal facts

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: At resonance X_L = X_C, φ = 0 and the power factor is 1. All of the average power is then the heating I_rms^2 R in the resistor. The inductor and capacitor still exchange energy, but their average contribution is zero.  ·  A power factor of zero means the current is 90° out of phase with the voltage, as in a pure inductor or a pure capacitor. Energy sloshes back to the source.  ·  A lagging power factor is the inductive case, common with motors. Capacitors are added in industry to pull the power factor back toward 1 so that the current, for a given useful power, is smaller.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Power factor is not the phase angle itself. It is the cosine.  ·  cosφ = R/Z, not Z/R.  ·  Resonance makes the power factor 1, not 0.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A high power factor means less reactive current, not a larger resistance by itself.  ·  Do not drop cosφ.  ·  R/Z cannot exceed 1.
